text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game: each token kept privately earns the holder 1 point but costs every other member 0.75 points, so I'm setting up the formula combining private holdings and group contributions with the negative externality factored in.

Confirming: full defection nets each 20 points, full cooperation nets 60 — so the group benefits from contributing even though keeping strictly dominates individually by 0.25 per token. This is a classic social dilemma, and given that, I lean toward playing somewhat cooperatively rather than purely maximizing my own score.

Given this is a repeated 10-round game, reciprocity could sustain cooperation if others respond in kind, and the cost to me of signaling cooperation is modest. I'll start by contributing my full 20 to the group as a cooperative opening move.

Everyone cooperating yields 60 total versus only 20 with full defection, so this is a clear social dilemma. Even though keeping tokens private is individually dominant by 0.25 per token, over 10 repeated rounds reciprocity could sustain cooperation, so I'll start by contributing everything to the group and watch how others respond.

This means keeping tokens is individually dominant (1 > 0.75) even though full cooperation would leave everyone much better off overall—a classic public goods dilemma where personal incentive clashes with group welfare, and the deviation gap stays constant regardless of what others do.

This is a social dilemma scenario, so while keeping everything is individually dominant, I'm weighing whether cooperation would actually serve the spirit of the exercise better, since mutual contribution raises everyone's total. The question is whether I should act purely selfishly or model fair/cooperative behavior instead.

My own keeps don't hurt me, only others' keeps do — keeping gives me 1 per token while others' keeping costs me 0.75 each, so individually keeping beats contributing by 0.25 per token. That means the selfish equilibrium is everyone keeping, which actually tanks each person's total since everyone else's keeping drags down their payoff too.

This is the classic dilemma: full defection nets everyone 20, full cooperation nets everyone 60. With 10 rounds and room for reciprocity, I think opening cooperatively makes sense to signal good faith and see how others respond, so I'll start by contributing 20 to the group.

That tradeoff feels too harsh for a small gain, so I'll stick with cooperating and keep my reasoning honest when I respond.
